speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: POSSIBLE RADIOACTIVE CONTAMINATION FOLLOWING PLANE CRASH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct this question to the
February 7, 1968

Inquiries of the Ministry Minister of Fisheries. In view of the statement by a British authority, Dr. Anthony Mi-chaelis, to the effect that the radioactive plutonium at the site of the crashed United States plane near Thule, Greenland may create a very serious danger to the fishing grounds off Newfoundland, may I ask the minister whether his department or any other department of the government is examining this potential danger and, if so, whether any action has been taken to prevent this if it is scientifically possible to do so?

subtopic: POSSIBLE RADIOACTIVE CONTAMINATION FOLLOWING PLANE CRASH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first may I advise the hon. member that the statement made by Dr. Mi-chaelis as reported by the Canadian Press is rather hypothetical. He said "if". It is not really based on actual fact.
After consultation with the experts of the Atomic Energy Control Board of Canada and the radiation protection division of the Department of National Health and Welfare, the oceanographers of the Fisheries Research Board have assured me that there is no possibility of any significant radioactive contamination, as a result of this incident, of any waters used by Canada or Canadian fisheries.

subtopic: POSSIBLE RADIOACTIVE CONTAMINATION FOLLOWING PLANE CRASH
speechtext: May I ask the minister whether any scientific team from his or any other department of government has visited the site of the unfortunate accident in order to assure themselves that every possible measure is being taken to prevent any danger to the fishing grounds off Newfoundland.

subtopic: POSSIBLE RADIOACTIVE CONTAMINATION FOLLOWING PLANE CRASH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot
assure the hon. member that such a team has visited the site, but as the hon. member is well aware my officials as well as the Atomic Energy Control Board of Canada and the radiation protection division of the Department of National Health and Welfare have been in contact with the proper authorities in this regard. Also, as I have stated, we have the assurance that there is no possibility of any radioactive reaction in waters this side of the Atlantic.

subtopic: POSSIBLE RADIOACTIVE CONTAMINATION FOLLOWING PLANE CRASH
speechtext: May I ask a further supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. What does the minister mean by his statement to the effect that the Atomic Energy Control Board has been in touch with the proper authorities? Does he mean the government of the United States and, if so, what branch of that government?

subtopic: POSSIBLE RADIOACTIVE CONTAMINATION FOLLOWING PLANE CRASH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not in a
position to tell the hon. member what branch, if any, of departments of the United States government has been contacted, but I am aware that the Atomic Energy Control Board has been following this incident since the bombs were dropped, and we have the assurance from them to the effect that there is no danger to our Canadian waters.

Mr. Speaker, on the motion for third reading of this bill I wish to move in amendment that the house go back into committee of the whole to correct a slight mistake in clause 28. This clause was not discussed in detail in committee of the whole. The trouble is that under this bill, when a licence is granted to the operator of a community antenna television operation he is required by the terms of the licence to maintain the integrity of all the programs received. He cannot alter a program. In fact he will not know what is coming over the air, since he is only a receiving station.
Many of the C.A.T.V. operators are licensed to receive programs from the United States. They must maintain the integrity of the program being broadcast. If some candidate or a supporter or opponent of a referendum in Canada chooses to advertise over a station in the United States, the program will come over community television in Canada and the operator can be brought into court under this clause 28 as it now stands.
I should like to move, in committee of the whole, that certain words be deleted from clause 28. The words which cover C.A.T.V. operators are "a receiving undertaking". I have been told that the situation is covered by the Canada Elections Act, section 99, subsection (2) which reads:
Every person who, with intent to influence persons to give or refrain from giving their votes at an election, uses, aids, abets, counsels or procures the use of any broadcasting station outside of Canada, during an election, for the broadcasting of any matter having reference to an election, is guilty of an illegal practice and of an offence against this act punishable on summary conviction as provided in this act.
This section does not cover the case of a citizen of the United States or a citizen of some other country than Canada, going on the air in the United States in an effort to influence the voting within 48 hours somewhere in Canada. Mr. Speaker, I shall detain the house but a few minutes to point out some of the views of the official opposition on this measure. I promise I will not go through any convolutions in which the members of a party support a motion and then do not vote for it, as the N.D.P. did when they forced a vote upon us within the last few minutes.
This measure, in the form of the white paper on broadcasting, came before the standing committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts in December, 1966. That committee made its report to the house in mid-March, 1967. Its proceedings will be found running from page 1342 to 2117 of the committee reports. Subsequently the measure was debated on second reading in the house and was further considered in committee of the whole. At least 90 per cent of the debate that took place on this very vital topic cannot be quarreled with, and speaking on behalf of my colleagues I can say we took as responsible a position as we possibly could toward a subject that is extraordinarily vexatious to a great number of Canadians. I will deal with the points of vexation a little later.
If we have a quarrel it is with the government. First and foremost there was its delay in appointing top officers to the C.B.C., and more particularly in filling the office of president, sometimes described as the second most important position in the country, second only to that of the office of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). Many months ago Mr. Oui-met indicated that he wished to retire as president, and we were confronted with the suggestion that his replacement should be appointed only after this bill had received parliamentary approval. Mr. Ouimet finally solved that dilemma by saying he was moving out willy-nilly, and subsequently new officers were appointed.
I suggest that during that time, when C.B.C. employees were under a great deal of stress, the government allowed to remain at the top level of the C.B.C. a vacuum which could only disturb the morale of the employees and prevent the C.B.C. from carrying out its responsibilities to the country. We had the example-and the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) tabled the correspondence the other day-of defiance continuing from within the middle ranks of the C.B.C.

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting To reinforce that point I refer to page 6127 of Hansard for January 29 and the text of a letter sent by a Mr. Claude Sylvestre, Secretary of the Association of Producers, to the Secretary of State on November 6. I quote from that letter because I think it is symptomatic of the viewpoint of some within the public service of Canada, within the C.B.C., who are defiant not only of their own top people but of the will of parliament. In his letter Mr. Sylvestre wrote:
We believe that our prime role, as producers, is to reflect and to interpret the living reality in a country. We do not believe that official government thinking is necessarily the kind of objective thinking which should be the basis of political and cultural information.
Note the clever use of the word "government", when he should really be saying that parliamentary thinking does not reflect the views of our country.
The C.B.C. is obliged to bring to light all forms of power in the sense that it must allow a confrontation of forces and debates on the relative values of any given society. If we are to be the vehicle for or to promote one political line then we are willingly conniving with an organ of propaganda.
What political line are they being asked to promote, Mr. Speaker? I think the political line, if that is the expression that must be used, is nothing less than the unity and selfpreservation of the country that all of us are sworn to serve in this chamber.
I continue to quote from the letter:
We have at all times refused to do so; we refuse to do so today, when what you are saying is in short that the Left will be tolerated on the condition that it be reactionary. And in this way our function as producers will remain while governments come and go.
That, sir, is a clear statement of defiance by an element that, for its numbers, has great importance in promoting ideas on a countrywide basis or on a very large regional basis.
The Secretary of State in what I thought was a good reply, dated November 10, quoted from Mr. R. B. Bennett who brought the original legislation dealing with the C.B.C. before this house many years ago. She quoted Mr. Bennett as follows:
Properly employed radio can be a most effective instrument in nation-building with an educational value difficult to estimate.
Farther on she quoted Mr. Bennett as follows:
Without such control radio broadcasting can never become a great agency for the communication of matters of national concern and for the diffusion of national thoughts and ideas and without such control it can never be the agency by

which national consciousness may be fostered and sustained and national unity still further strengthened.
Sir, the word down through the years, from the wisdom of that particular statesman through royal commissions, committees of inquiry, parliamentary committees and the like, has been that the C.B.C. can be and should be a great weapon in fostering national identity and national purpose. I only wish that the Secretary of State had been a little less ladylike in replying to Mr. Sylvstre's group and had told them where to go in very short order. I think this was defiance. Further, I think it was defiance that perhaps the Secretary of State and the government brought on themselves simply by failing, when Mr. Ouimet became a lame-duck president, to appoint somebody who would step in and clear up that very gray and uncertain area that exists between top management of the C.B.C. and the group at the producers' level.
While the government has procured two people who in the long run will undoubtedly prove their value and service as the chief broadcasting executives of the C.B.C., still there must be something seriously amiss with the corporation if those appointments could not have come from within its own ranks. I think the C.B.C. should be a place where people can embark on long-term careers, starting at no matter what level but always having the chance to reach the top. It is a matter of personal regret to me, considering the series of crises which have beset the C.B.C. over the last few years, that apparently nobody at the top level was considered of sufficient merit to be appointed to either one of the two topmost posts.
Changes were made in this bill during its consideration in committee of the whole, and I would be remiss if I did not thank the Secretary of State for being amenable to three changes that seemed of particular interest and value to my colleagues and myself. Changes were made in clause 2 covering the important declaration of principles dealing with the national system and the private system. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) proposed one of the changes and I a second, both of which were accepted, and for that we are grateful to the minister.
A change was also made in the penalty clause. To us it seemed important that we should not stigmatize this industry, and I

think the minister made an obeisance to common sense when she agreed to that change.
The major change was the deletion of clause 47, which had been the subject of considerable palaver behind the scenes, thus saving days and days of debate. Again the official opposition is grateful to the minister for deleting that clause dealing with five-year budgets. We must be jealous of the right of parliament to exercise control, and therefore I think that by and large we have mollified the worst features in this legislation.

However, I believe there are still areas of weakness which remain in what we as a parliament have done. I do not think we have met head on the expansion problem, the extension of radio and television service to Canadians who either do not receive it now in any shape or form or who receive only one type of service and would like the advantage of having freedom of choice. I do not believe we have resolved the concern of many Canadians who believe there should be more effective control within the public system on the part of top management with regard to those who are on the production line. Indeed, the minister herself has referred to rotten management within the C.B.C. In that area we can only hope that Dr. Davidson, a good sensible Nova Scotian, and Mr. Picard from Montreal will be able to come to grips rapidly with problems which of this type have been raised by several hon. members.
Third, I do not think we have really solved the problem of parliamentary control of the budget of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Millions of Canadians have never had the idea sold to them properly-indeed, many parliamentarians have not either-why the corporation should use such a large amount of public funds. These three areas of challenge face the new officers. As I say, the Conservative opposition wish them well in the discharge of their duties. However, until we can see the results in these three areas we still have to be convinced that this legislation is in the best interests of the public.

Mr. Speaker, I will ignore the opening observation of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) about the division. It seems to me that a comment of this nature is the last thing which should come from the ranks of the official opposition. The government has put off, temporarily I hope, the question of five-year financing for the C.B.C. The minister said there will be a separate bill on that
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting subject later. In the interval I hope that members who have some doubts about five-year financing will use the time to frame other proposals. Five years may be too long a period but I think one year is too short. Some period such as two years or three years will, I trust, be agreed upon eventually. I think the important point in respect of any large organization, whether it be the C.B.C. or indeed another government department or crown corporation, is that for both capital and operating purposes the financing should be for a period of longer than one year.
There is a tendency here to do things simply because they have been done in the past. It has been our custom to examine and pass the estimates of every department and agency each year. I hope that in time this practice may change. It would be no great blow to democracy. I point out to hon. members that in the United States the state legislatures meet only once every two years and pass the budget then for that period. In the United Kingdom the British Broadcasting Corporation never comes to parliament for money because it has other means of financing. I believe that any organization as big as the C.B.C. or, indeed, as big as many government departments, could operate more efficiently if the officials knew what the financing of the organization would be for a period of two or three years. We may reach the point where the estimates of departments, agencies and crown corporations will go on a three-year cycle. This would mean that we would examine one-third of them each year. Perhaps this would mean that there would be a more searching examination than there is at the present time.
When we deal with estimates here we do not actually go into the separate items in great detail. We use the time devoted to the consideraion of the estimates as an opportunity to make speeches on various subjects. We all do this and it seems to be a defensible practice. But the actual detailed spending receives very little close scrutiny. I suggest that in future we might adopt this other method of operation. speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CALENDAR, FINANCIAL AND PREMIUM YEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize for having kept my hon. friends waiting for a few moments but I was detained in my office by a true blue supporter of the Conservative party who wanted to meet me.
Mr. Speaker, we are now on second reading of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act. The main object of the bill is to amend the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act with a view to allowing it to co-ordinate the deposit insurance granted under its terms with deposit insurance granted under any provincial deposit insurance plan.
Under the terms of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act, which was passed earlier this year, the deposits entrusted to banks, trusts and loan companies incorporated under federal acts are insured within the statutory limits. The corporation is also authorized to issue insurance policies to institutions incorporated under provincial acts, with the agreement of the province of incorporation, the deposits entrusted to those institutions being insured to the same extent as those entrusted to federal institutions.
At the present time, the act requires that every deposit of a member institution shall be insured within the limits provided in the act. The corporation is not authorized to insure only certain deposits of the member institution to the exclusion of others. It cannot insure deposits in some provinces to the exclusion of deposits in other provinces.
Since the passage of this legislation earlier this year, the province of Quebec has established a deposit insurance plan which applies to all deposits accepted in Quebec by the institutions which accept deposits and transact business in that province. The administrative authority, the Quebec deposit insurance board, is also authorized to insure deposits accepted outside Quebec by institutions incorporated in Quebec.
In order to reduce to a minimum the duplication of coverage, costs and inspection
February 7, 1968

between the federal and the provincial plans, in the case of an institution covered by both, discussions were held between officials of the federal government and of the government of the province of Quebec. This matter has also been discussed in June by officials during a federal-provincial meeting dealing with financial institutions. The agreement arrived at following these discussions was summed up in an exchange of letters between the Minister of Finance and the premier of Quebec, letters which have been tabled in the house on July 9. This bill is mainly intended to allow for the implementation of this agreement.
The following are the main provisions of the agreement: with regard to institutions incorporated in the province of Quebec, the Quebec deposit insurance board will insure deposits in the province, and the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation will insure deposits outside of the province. With regard to institutions incorporated in the other provinces and exercizing their activities in Quebec, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, with the consent of the province of origin, will insure all deposits other than those made in Quebec, and the Quebec deposit insurance board will insure deposits made in Quebec. This provision requires that the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation be authorized to insure not all but some of the deposits of a member institution, and it will be granted this power by the present amendment. The amendment will also allow the corporation to enter into agreements with the province of Quebec or, as the case may be, with the Quebec deposit insurance board, in order to co-ordinate the two plans. Those agreements will have to deal with several questions, such as the definition of the location of a deposit. The amendment will also enable the governor in council to pass regulations, as needed, in order to authorize the corporation to comply with the provisions of those co-ordinating agreements when they are not provided for in the legislation. There is also the authority to exchange information concerning provincial institutions insured both by the corporation and by the Quebec deposit insurance board.
Although the main object of the bill is to enable the Corporation to co-ordinate its insurance with the insurance of the Quebec deposit insurance board, the amendment has been drafted in general terms, so that similar arrangements may be concluded with any province which may have established a deposit insurance system.
Canada Deposit Insurance Act
As far as the federally chartered institutions are concerned, the federal government has already assumed the responsibility of setting up financial and control requirements. A very exhaustive system of regulation and control has been in force for a long time. Deposits entrusted to those institutions are insured under a statutory provision of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act. We therefore believe that each province should accept the control and insurance which apply to those institutions under federal legislation. The provinces should not add the insurance or the inspection provided for in their own legislation. The amendment applies therefore only to the insurance of provincial institutions and not to that of federal institutions.
During the discussions between officials, it was recognized that when a province adopts a deposit insurance scheme, the insurance of the institutions incorporated under provincial legislation can create problems only if, following a lack of premium revenue, the adequate reserves cannot be constituted, except over a long period of time. To remove that difficulty, it was agreed during the discussions that, provided the authorization is granted by parliament, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation will be willing to grant short-term loans, against sufficient security, to a provincial agency entrusted with the administration of a deposit insurance scheme in order to allow that agency to meet shortterm liquidity requirements. It was felt that this auxiliary supply of liquidity would enable the province to adopt and administer a scheme with lower reserves and revenue than would otherwise be necessary. It would be understood that these short-term loans would be consistent with agreements concluded between the corporation and the provincial agency and would be granted provided the province refrained from levying a tax or establishing a system of premiums which would cause expenses to federal chartered institutions as far as deposit insurance in the province is concerned, where deposits are already insured by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The amendment under consideration will permit the corporation to extend such shortterm loans, subject to terms and conditions provided by the governor in council and to an agreement which will also have to be approved by the governor in council.
Another subject dealt with in the amending bill is technical; it would provide a better method than the one now provided in the act
6474	COMMONS
Canada Deposit Insurance Act to assess the premium of any member institution for the year during which it becomes a member institution.
The amending bill describes the premium year as running from the first of May to the 30th of April of the next year and provides that, for the premium year during which an institution became a member institution, a premium on a prorata basis will be payable for the period of the premium year to run at the time the institution becomes member institution. This amendment provides a more equitable method than the one now in the act and will clear up any doubt as far as the premium payable for the first year of deposit insurance is concerned.
An amendment allows the corporation to approve methods for calculating the total amount of deposits serving as a basis for premiums. This provision has given rise to a few technical difficulties, since only deposits to a maximum of $20,000 per person with each institution are covered by deposit insurance. An institution must therefore co-ordinate its obligations toward every person individually, in order to know the exact amount of insured deposits for the calculation of premiums. In view of the practical problems raised by such calculations, it has been deemed advisable to allow the use of approximate methods. Under its regulations, the corporation recognizes an approximate method in calculating the appropriate total. Under a proposed amendment, the corporation is authorized to use or accept approximate methods which may prove suitable.
The bill contains a further amendment providing for the permanent insurance of deposits entrusted by a person to two or more member institutions which have merged. At the present time, the act provides for a maximum insurance of $20,000 per depositor in any institution. Where a depositor has deposits in more than one member institution, he can be covered in each of them up to a maximum of $20,000. Were the act not amended, the merging of two member institutions could result in reducing the maximum deposit insurance of $20,000 granted a depositor in each of the two merging institutions, to a $20,000 maximum insurance with the new institution after the merger. The amendment will provide that the deposits taken over at the time of the merger will remain insured in the new institution. Therefore, the depositor will not see his deposits go without insurance because of the merger. The money entrusted after the merger by a person to the remaining

DEBATES	February 7. 1988
institution will not be insured as long as the total amount of the deposits of that person taken over at the time of the merger does not fall below $20,000.
At present, the corporation defines the term "deposit" by regulation, subject to the approval of the governor in council. A provision in the present bill will abolish the right to modify the definition of the term "deposit" by a regulation of the corporation after one year from the day when the present bill comes into force. Any change in the definition of the term "deposit" made after that date will require a special act of parliament. This provision was added to the bill by an amendment presented by the Senate committee on banking and commerce. The government believes that the present procedure in order to define the term "deposit" and change the definition will do for a while yet; therefore, it did not suggest that the definition of the term "deposit" be established by the act. However, the government is not opposed to this change in the bill as it allows the present method to remain in force for another year.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the remarks made by the Minister of Fisheries in connection with the proposed amendments to the Fish Inspection Act. Generally speaking, the people in the fishing industry, as represented by the Fisheries Council of Canada and in my home province of Nova Scotia by the Fish Packers Association, are in agreement with the amendments proposed in this bill. Quite rightly, the people engaged in the fishing industry are proud of the fact that they have in the past been shipping fancy quality fish and fish products not only to all parts of Canada and to the east and west coasts of the United States but also to the United Kingdom, Europe and Australia. It is in their best interests that the Fish Inspection Act be clear and concise so that it will assure quality fish being shipped by Canadian processors not only to their markets in Canada but to their export markets as well, and also that fish and fish products shipped into this country are up to our standards of quality.
February 7, 1968

The first amendment is of a minor nature. It simply expands the meaning of the word "container" as defined in the original Fish Inspection Act to include the wrapper or confining band used in the packing or marketing of fish. I can understand the necessity for this change in wording because marketing procedures for some types of fish have changed considerably since the 1949 Fish Inspection Act was introduced. I refer here to the packaging of dry salted cod which used to be marketed in large wooden boxes and sold in bulk quantity at the retail level. At the moment, confining bands are also used in the marketing of whole lobsters and crabs which have been cooked and frozen. I therefore agree with the proposal to amend this section. In clause 1, paragraph (h)-

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, I appreciate your suggestion and I shall endeavour to confine my remarks to the principle of the bill. I had hoped to deal briefly, since I believe I will be the only speaker for our party on this measure, with some of the clauses. If you will bear with me, Mr. Speaker, since the clauses are not too contentious, I should like to refer to clause 1, paragraph (h), the amendment which proposes expanding the meaning of the word "processing" to include the canning of fish. This also seems to me to be a valid change since the canning of fish all over Canada plays a very important role in the marketing of our fisheries products. We have only to think of our vast salmon canning industry, as well as our tuna, lobster, herring, mackerel, clams, fish cakes,
Fish Inspection Act
sardines and cat food, to realize the vast importance of the canning of fish to the industry as a whole. As we search for ever greater markets for our fish products, this aspect of the industry will play an ever increasing role. In my opinion, fish canning should be included under processing.
I now come to the final amendment in this short bill. This amendment changes the words in section 10 from the original wording, which was:
No person shall import, export, sell for export or have in his possession for export any fish intended for human consumption unless the fish is wholesome and fit for human food.
The new wording of the section reads:
No person shall import, export, sell for export or have in his possession for export any fish intended for human consumption that is tainted, decomposed or unwholesome.
I should like to state at once, Mr. Speaker, that I agree with the intent of this amendment. Certainly no one with any interest in the fishing industry could approve of shipping fish for human consumption that was tainted, decomposed or unwholesome.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
The fishing industry at the present time is going through a very trying and difficult period. The high labour and operating costs which are affecting other industries are also having their effect on the fishing industry, and the situation is so desperate that only the strongest financially backed fishing companies can hope to survive. This condition has been brought about by an increase in fishing activity without a resultant expansion in our markets. Fish processors have also found it practically impossible to pass on their increasing costs of procuring, processing and packaging, and high interest, marketing and transport charges, when selling their product in competition with the product of other countries in which costs are obviously lower.
The fact that those who follow the Roman Catholic faith are no longer required to eat fish on Friday has had a damaging effect on the marketing of our fish and fish products, both in Canada and in the United States. When one considers these facts and realizes that Canadians per capita, only consume about 13 pounds of fish annually, one realizes the extent of the marketing problem that faces our industry.
Somehow Canadians must be made to realize that seafood offers them top value in today's high-priced economy. When you buy at the retail level one pound of fish fillets for 69 cents you are getting 16 ounces of protein

February 7, 1968
Fish Inspection Act
without any fat or bone. There is absolutely no waste, and at the same time you are giving your family valuable minerals and protection against goiter through the iodine content of salt water fish. It is also well known that doctors recommend that those who are overweight or suffer from heart disease eat more fish and cut down on starchy, fatty foods.
With all these factors to encourage the increased consumption of fish there should be little difficulty in marketing our fish production. But apparently we have fallen down in our efforts to teach Canadians the proper methods of preparing fish. I know that the fisheries department, through its cooking school, has been active in this regard; fish recipes have been brought forward. Nevertheless, more must be done. Perhaps we should borrow a page from the French in this regard. They place more emphasis on the cooking and preparation of fish than on the cooking and preparation of meat in their diet. One of the first steps we must take is, of course, to ensure that our fish arrives at market in A-l condition, and to ensure that is the purpose of this amendment.
While I do not disagree with the intent of the amendment there are one or two matters relevant to the act which I wish to point out to the minister.
The Fish Inspection Act of 1949 and the regulations under it cover a large area. The act has wide powers. From reading sections 4 and 5 we gain some idea of the heavy responsibilities that are placed on the shoulders of our fish inspectors. Section 4 of the act reads as follows:
4.	(1) An Inspector may at any time
(a) enter any place or premises, or any steamship, vessel or boat, or any railway car, truck, carriage, car, aircraft or other vehicle used for the carriage or storage of fish and may open any container that he has reason to believe contains fish,
(b)	require to be produced for inspection or for the purpose of obtaining copies thereof or extracts therefrom any books, shipping bills, bills of lading, or other documents or papers, and
(c)	take any samples for inspection.
Section 5 reads:
5.	A person interested in a decision of an inspector in respect of any inspection, grading, marking or other matter under this Part or the regulations thereunder may appeal to the Minister in accordance with the procedure prescribed by the Governor in Council.
There is no provision in the act for an appeal, except to the minister. Of course,

when you are dealing with a perishable product like fish this procedure takes much valuable time which one can ill afford.
Sections 6 and 7 of the act read as follows:
6.	For the purposes of this Part, inspectors may administer oaths and take and receive affidavits, declarations and affirmations.
7.	(1) Whenever an inspector believes on reasonable grounds that an offence against this Part or any regulation thereunder has been committed, he may seize all fish and containers by means of or in relation to which he reasonably believes the offence was committed.
(2)	All fish and containers seized pursuant to subsection (1) may be detained for a period of two months following the day of seizure, unless during that period proceedings under this Part in respect of those fish and containers are undertaken, in which case the fish and containers may be further detained until such proceedings are finally concluded.
(3)	Where a person is convicted of an offence against this Part or any regulation thereunder, the fish and containers by means of or in relation to which the offence was committed, upon such conviction, in addition to any penalty imposed, are forfeited to Her Majesty and may be disposed of as the Minister may direct.
These sections are pertinent to our discussion since they contain the only authority under which an inspector can enforce the changes which are contained in the new subsection 1 of section 10 as set out in clause 3 of the bill. For example, let us assume that an inspector takes a sample of fish for inspection and as a result of his analysis he condemns the shipment. We must ascertain the conditions under which the tests were made. Was the fish sample, for instance, taken on Friday afternoon? Was it placed in the trunk of a car and then conveyed to a fish inspection site on Saturday? The place may have been closed and it may be that the fish was not examined until the following Monday. Section 4(c) of the act says that the inspector may at any time "take any samples for inspection". But the act does not say whether he must put this sample on ice or take it immediately for inspection. These matters are not spelled out, and they should be spelled out more clearly. Also, if the inspector were vindictive he could put a fish processor out of business by being seemingly overzealous in carrying out his duties. This, of course, would be tantamount to an outright fraud perpetrated by the federal government on the fishing industry. I agree with the intent of this bill but I am concerned about abuses that might arise under the powers that are granted to fish inspectors.

In view of my concern and the concern of some men in the industry with whom I have discussed this matter, I think the minister should give thought to bringing in further amendments to this act. An inspector may board a boat, seize it and hold the fish until they rot. He can do this without a warrant and the owner has no right of redress. He cannot claim compensation and is not entitled to take advantage of due process of law as granted by the Bill or Rights. It was certainly my hope that we could apply the safeguards contained in the Bill of Rights to the provisions of the Fish Inspection Act. This would prevent repetition of many of the abuses which have taken place in the past.
I agree with the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) that the amendments proposed here are of a minor character. In one instance we are concerned only with a change in technology. I am sure that the Bill of Rights could legitimately have been applied in this field so as to limit the authority of the inspection branch of the Department of Fisheries and see to it that the work is done with a greater sense of responsibility toward the various interests concerned. the second reading of Bill No. S-23, to amend the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act and the Criminal Code.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the amendments contained in this bill cover two separate matters. The first group of amendments provides for the introduction of a pure nickel coinage in place of our present silver alloy coinage. The second provides authority for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) to invest some of the resources of the exchange fund account in certain short term securities of the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
Hon. members may recall that on December 23,	1966, the Minister of Finance
February 7, 1968	COMMONS
announced that the government intended to change from a silver coinage to a pure nickel coinage some time during 1968, and that proposals to amend the Mint, Currency and Exchange Fund Act would be presented to parliament to authorize this change. The reason for making an advance announcement of our intentions, of course, was to give the automatic vending industry and other interested parties time to make the necessary arrangements required to cope with a new coinage.
Before dealing with these matters it might be helpful if I were to explain why it became necessary to plan to abandon the use of silver in the coinage and to use pure nickel in its place. As the Minister of Finance said last year, this decision was forced upon us by events over which the government of Canada had no control. We have had a silver coinage since the early years of confederation, and during the last century there has been virtually no change in the coins. The problem today is that silver has become a scarce commodity. There is very little increase in annual production year by year, but a large increase in demand.
Apart from the traditional uses of silver, the increase in demand has resulted in part from the many new industrial uses found for this metal. As a result of the growing scarcity of silver, most countries have found it necessary in the last several decades to abandon the use of silver in favour of less scarce and less expensive coinage materials, so that Canada is now one of the few countries in the world still maintaining a silver coinage. However, the increasing scarcity of silver was not a problem until about three years ago, when it became apparent that the reserves of silver maintained by the United States were being depleted more rapidly than heretofore. This meant that the ceiling price of $1.29 per ounce was bound to be exposed to strong upward pressures, thereby making silver uneconomic as a coinage material.
In the face of this situation the government of the United States in 1965 announced its intention to discontinue the minting of silver coins and began to issue coins made of cupronickel and copper toward the end of the same year. Since the new laminated United States coins performed in exactly the same way as silver alloy coins when used in coin machines -and, of course, their unusual construction was decided upon with this end in mind-the change-over raised no difficulties with respect to coin machines. For our part, we felt that
DEBATES	6485
Amendments Respecting Composition of Coins coins made of a homogeneous metal or alloy would be more attractive than a laminated coin, and our researches into the suitability of various alternative metals led to the choice of nickel.
We have been pleased to observe that there have been no doubts expressed by the Canadian people as to the suitability of pure nickel as a replacement for the silver alloy used in the coinage. The new coins will be reasonably similar in appearance and ring to our present coins. The nickel counterparts of the two silver coins most widely used, that is, the 10-cent and 25-cent pieces, of course will have exactly the same dimensions as the present coins and will be roughly similar in weight. Since pure nickel is a harder material than silver alloy, the new coins will wear better and will resist corrosion more effectively. Indeed, experience with the use of 5cent nickel coins since 1922 has already demonstrated that nickel is eminently suitable for use as coinage. At the same time, having regard to the pre-eminence of Canada as a nickel producer, its wider use in our coinage is most appropriate.
The only problem created by the changeover to nickel coins arises from the widespread use of coins in the vending machine business, and from the fact that the coin selectors used in them are designed to reject magnetic metals, including nickel. In the last few decades, and particularly in the last few years, the sale of goods and services by means of vending machines has become quite large. It is estimated that there are between 400,000 and 500,000 of these machines in Canada carrying a relatively sophisticated coin selector for the purpose of testing the genuineness of the coins.

It is also desirable, of course, in the interest of the tourist trade at points on our border with the United States, that such replacement selectors should be able to accept

As a result, various manufacturers have now designed new types of coin selectors which it is expected will meet the requirements that I have just mentioned. A firm of management consultants has been engaged by the department to investigate and report upon the availability of new coin selectors and the time required to instal a sufficient number of them in vending machines. I would expect that after this report has been received and studied, perhaps within the next month or so, I will be able to give a more firm advance notice of the date on which the mint will begin issuing the new nickel coins. I would also expect to announce the decision of the government concerning proposals for compensation. The department is now exploring the practical feasibility, as well as the desirability, of compensating these vending machine operators for a part of the expense that they will incur in replacing their present coin selectors with new ones.
An explanation concerning some of the coins described in part II of the schedule may be helpful. Hon. members will recall that on August 18 last the Minister of Finance announced that for a short period a special issue of 10-cent and 25-cent coins containing 50 per cent silver and 50 per cent copper would be issued. Up until then our coins contained 80 per cent silver. This change was made necessary by the increase in the price of silver which took place at that time after the United States lifted the ceiling on the price of silver. These new silver coins will continue to be issued by the mint until such time as we are ready to begin issuing nickel coins later


this year. They are therefore included in the schedule along with the proposed nickel coins.
We are also providing authority in the bill for the issuance of 50-cent and one dollar coins containing 50 per cent silver to cover the possibility that we might wish to mint such coins in the future for numismatic purposes only.
Our discussions with the representatives of the automatic merchandising industry have led to the suggestion that it would be sensible to take advantage of the opportunity presented by the change-over to a nickel coinage to reduce the size of our 50-cent and one dollar coins. The present coins are regarded by the public as being too bulky to be carried around. It was therefore felt that a reduction in the size of these two coins, and particularly that of the 50 cent piece, might turn out to be a convenience to the public and probably to the vending industry. With this in mind, and after consulting with various interested groups, the bill proposes that the weight and size of the 50-cent and one dollar coins made of nickel will be somewhat smaller than the present coins of the same values.
One other amendment should be mentioned. The existing statute establishes the Royal Canadian Mint in Ottawa. The present bill proposes that the mint may be established anywhere within the national capital region. This change is intended to give the government a greater freedom with respect to the possible relocation of the mint. We intend to build a new mint in the next few years to replace the present structure which was built in 1908 and is now overcrowded and inefficient. A modem factory-type building will enable the mint to produce a larger output of coins without resorting to shift work, and also enable it to seek some export business, as it should. No decision has yet been taken on a new location.
I would like now to turn to the two amendments which deal with the exchange fund. This is a special account in the name of the Minister of Finance in which the government holds most of its foreign exchange assets, that is, its gold and U.S. dollars.
Under the act at present the minister may purchase with money in the account (a) gold; (b) U.S. currency, U.S. dollar bank deposits or treasury bills or other obligations of the United States; (c) other currencies freely convertible into gold or U.S. dollars and deposits in these currencies; (d) securities of or guaranteed by the government of Canada; and (e) securities of the International Monetary Fund
February 7, 1968

maturing not later than five years from their date of issue. These latter securities are issued by the I.M.F. in connection with our obligation under the "general arrangements to borrow" to provide, along with the nine other most industrialized member countries of the I.M.F., up to $6 billion of additional resources to the I.M.F.
The bill before the house will broaden somewhat the investment powers of the exchange fund. Clause 5 of the bill will amend the act to enable the fund to purchase securities of the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development maturing not later than two years from their date of issue.
The securities which the exchange fund would expect to purchase with this authority are the special issues of two-year central bank bonds which the I.B.R.D. first brought out in 1964 and which are offered only to central banks and other government institutions. These bonds are denominated in U.S. currency and are offered every six months. The last issue was on September 15, 1967 and was sold to central banks and other governmental institutions in 43 countries and to one international organization. The issue was for $100 million U.S. and paid an interest of 5f per cent. The characteristics of these bonds and their attractive yields make them an appropriate investment for some of the money in the exchange fund.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
In addition, they offer a vehicle for us to provide some further financial support to the International Bank, support well warranted by the bank's success and effectiveness in the field of economic development. With the tightness in capital markets of the world and the bank's desire for additional loanable funds, the bank has been encouraging more governments and governmental institutions to invest in these securities. In this amendment we have an excellent opportunity to serve directly Canada's interest by providing an attractive alternative investment for the exchange fund and at the same time assisting the I.B.R.D. in its important work in the field of economic development.
The second amendment to this part of the act is technical in nature. The present act provides for the transfer to the consolidated revenue fund at the end of each year of that portion of the exchange fund's net income derived from interest and discounts on the securities held in its portfolio. It does not
Amendments Respecting Composition of Coins provide, however, for the transfer of other income realized by the exchange fund, most of which is derived from trading operations.
The Auditor General and the public accounts committee of this house recommended the transfer of these other profits to the consolidated revenue fund, and the Department of Finance undertook to obtain the necessary authority. While we were awaiting an opportunity to open up this act for amendment we did, in fact, obtain the authority by an item in supplementary estimates (A) for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1968, vote 23a. This vote authorized the transfer of these other profits for the calendar year 1964 and subsequent years. The amendment in clause 6 of the bill before us will supersede this item.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: LEGISLATIVE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COMPOSITION OF COINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring forward once again a matter that I brought to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) on the orders of the day a few weeks ago. I refer to the frustration experienced by the Canadian people as a result of their inability to procure by purchase 50-cent pieces and dollars as mementoes of the celebration of the Canadian centennial. I have been told on good authority that these are available but not to the general Canadian public. There are people who have large amounts of these 50-cent pieces and dollars. For example, a large well known retail firm in this country is offering 50-cent pieces for sale but you have to pay $3 for them. As a result of the way the distribution of these 50-cent pieces and dollars has been managed the Canadian public is being rooked.
Consequent upon the change-over from silver to the new metal, about which the minister has advised us, people are not able to purchase these coins. Not only from the firm I have mentioned in Canada but if you write to Iola, Wisconsin, you can get silver dollars or 50-cent pieces. If you write to Turner, Montana, you can also get 50-cent pieces. As a matter of fact, in the Numismatic News for January 29, 1968, the heading on page 31 reads: "Less than 1 per cent of the people in the United States and Canada will ever own a Canadian commemorative centennial set of coins". The article reads in part:
This is one of the most highly recommended sets with a solid future. Do you realize that many Canadians have never seen a set, let alone own one? They have been waiting for their banks to get these coins but the mint was forced to stop regular minting of dollars and halves early in the year because silver was worth more than their face value. With 1967 now gone, no bank will have them

February 7, 1968
Business of the House
but the public still wants them. Yes. the prices have been going up because of greater demand than supply and prices will continue to rise as supplies are getting smaller every day. You can test this yourself by just advertising to buy, and if you have any luck in buying please sell us your surplus. We need rolls and sets.
I quote from an advertisement in this newspaper:
We made a fortunate purchase 1 Would you like some truly Gem BU Dollars and halves of 1967? These have never seen the inside of a bag. These are just as they came off the coining presses. Limited supply-only two rolls of each per order. True Gem 1967 dollars, $77.50 per roll; true Gem 1967 half dollars, $77.50 per roll.
You can obtain these coins by writing to Turner, Montana. People have to pay these exorbitant prices simply because of the mismanagement and lack of foresight of the government in assuring that the coins were not sold in huge lots to foreign purchasers so that Canadians could be rooked if they desired a centennial dollar or 50-cent piece. You can write to Bloomington, Illinois, and obtain these coins. This firm is selling Canadian dollars at $55 per roll and half dollars at $75 per roll. There are Canadian proof-like rolls of half dollars available at $72 per roll. I must say that I feel this is another example of mismanagement of the country's affairs by this government.
